title: How does the JDK Flow API relate to Project Reactor and RxJava? They all implement the same Reactive Streams contract: so when do you choose a reactive library over `CompletableFuture`, and when do virtual threads make reactive unnecessary?
shortTitle: Flow API vs Reactor vs RxJava?
keyPoints: Flow API, Reactor, and RxJava all implement the same Reactive Streams specification and interoperate.
Flow has no operators; Reactor (Flux/Mono) and RxJava (Flowable/Observable) add map, filter, flatMap.
CompletableFuture models a single async value, not a backpressured stream of many items.
Virtual threads (Java 21) let blocking code scale cheaply, removing much of the reason for reactive.
Choose reactive for continuous streams with backpressure: SSE, Kafka pipelines, WebSocket fan-out.
Choose CompletableFuture for a single async result or a handful of parallel calls to fan out and join.
Reactive and virtual threads are not mutually exclusive: reactive wins for true streaming, virtual threads win for request-per-task.

s1_definition.oneliner: Flow, Reactor and RxJava speak the same Reactive Streams contract; reactive is for backpressured streams, CompletableFuture is for a single async result, and virtual threads let simple blocking code scale so you only go reactive when you truly need streaming backpressure.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Flow API** – the lowest common denominator: four interfaces, no operators, no runtime.
- **Reactor** – `Flux<T>` (0..N items) and `Mono<T>` (0..1 item) with a rich operator set, used by Spring WebFlux.
- **RxJava** – `Flowable<T>` (backpressured) and `Observable<T>` (no backpressure) with operators and schedulers.
- **CompletableFuture** – models a single asynchronous value with composition (`thenApply`, `thenCompose`, `thenCombine`).
- **Virtual threads (Java 21)** – lightweight threads that make blocking code scale cheaply, removing much of the concurrency motivation for reactive.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the Reactive Streams contract as the standard shape of a cheque that every bank in India agrees on. The Flow API is the bare blank cheque: valid, but you fill everything by hand. Reactor and RxJava are pre-printed cheque books with helpful boxes (operators). `CompletableFuture` is a single demand draft: one amount, one payee. Virtual threads are like hiring ten thousand cheap tellers so you can just let each customer wait at a counter, without the reactive machinery at all.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Reactive Streams Specification (4 interfaces)
       │
  ┌────┴────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                      │
  ▼                                      ▼
  Flow API              Reactor / RxJava
  (bare interfaces)     (interfaces + operators)
  no map, filter        map, filter, flatMap,
  no runtime            retry, window, buffer

  CompletableFuture        Virtual Threads
  (single async value)     (blocking code that scales)
  thenApply, thenCombine   Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()
  no backpressure          no reactive overhead

  Decision:
  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Stream + back-   │  │ Single value     │  │ Blocking I/O     │
  │ pressure needed? │  │ or fan-out?      │  │ at scale?        │
  │ → Reactor/RxJava │  │ → CompletableFut │  │ → Virtual threads│
  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The JDK Flow API, Project Reactor, and RxJava all implement the identical Reactive Streams specification. The Flow interfaces are the lowest common denominator with no operators at all. Reactor with Flux and Mono, and RxJava with Flowable, add the rich operator libraries.

I choose a reactive library when the problem is genuinely a continuous stream that needs backpressure and rich operators. I choose CompletableFuture when I have a single asynchronous result or a handful of independent calls to fan out and join. The biggest shift is virtual threads in Java 21, which let me write blocking code that scales, removing much of the reason to go reactive for thread efficiency.

At National Bank of India I now pick by the shape of the problem: reactive for the settlement feed that needs backpressure, CompletableFuture for the dashboard that fans out two calls, and virtual threads for the batch processor that runs blocking I/O at scale.

Remember one sentence: Flow, Reactor, and RxJava share the Reactive Streams contract; use reactive for backpressured streams, CompletableFuture for a single value, and virtual threads when blocking code needs to scale.
